title.value: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

abstract.value: Deeper neural networks are more difficult to train. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence showing that these residual networks are easier to optimize, and can gain accuracy from considerably increased depth. On the ImageNet dataset we evaluate residual nets with a depth of up to 152 layers—8× deeper than VGG nets [41] but still having lower complexity. An ensemble of these residual nets achieves 3.57% error on the ImageNet test set. This result won the 1st place on the ILSVRC 2015 classification task. We also present analysis on CIFAR-10 with 100 and 1000 layers. The depth of representations is of central importance for many visual recognition tasks. Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset. Deep residual nets are foundations of our submissions to ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions, where we also won the 1st places on the tasks of ImageNet detection, ImageNet localization, COCO detection, and COCO segmentation.

research_problem.value: As neural networks become deeper, their accuracy can saturate and then degrade, with deeper plain networks sometimes showing higher training error than shallower networks. This degradation is not simply caused by overfitting and indicates that conventional stacked layers become difficult to optimize. The paper addresses this degradation problem by introducing residual learning, which makes it easier to train substantially deeper networks.

methodology.value: The authors introduce residual learning, in which stacked layers learn a residual function F(x) = H(x) - x rather than directly learning the underlying mapping H(x). Shortcut connections add the input to the output of the stacked layers; when dimensions increase, they use either zero-padded identity shortcuts or projection shortcuts. The networks are trained end-to-end with stochastic gradient descent and evaluated on image classification, detection, and localization. The paper studies ResNets of 18, 34, 50, 101, and 152 layers on ImageNet, and CIFAR-10 networks from 20 to 1202 layers.

dataset.value: The experiments use ImageNet for image classification, detection, and localization; CIFAR-10 for classification and analysis of very deep networks; PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012 for object detection; and MS COCO for object detection. The ImageNet experiments use the 1000-class classification dataset, while the CIFAR-10 experiments use 50,000 training images and 10,000 test images across 10 classes.

reported_results.value: An ensemble of residual networks achieves 3.57% top-5 error on the ImageNet classification test set, winning first place in ILSVRC 2015. The single ResNet-152 model achieves 4.49% top-5 error on the ImageNet validation set. On CIFAR-10, ResNet-110 achieves 6.43% test error, while the 1202-layer network achieves 7.93%. On MS COCO, ResNet-101 improves the standard detection metric mAP@[.5, .95] by 6.0 percentage points over VGG-16, a 28% relative improvement. The competition ensemble achieves 37.4 mAP@[.5, .95] on the test-dev set. On PASCAL VOC, the enhanced ResNet-101 system achieves 85.6% mAP on VOC 2007 and 83.8% mAP on VOC 2012. On ImageNet detection, an ensemble achieves 62.1% mAP on the test set. On ImageNet localization, an ensemble achieves 9.0% top-5 localization error on the test set.

value: The 1202-layer ResNet reaches training error similar to the 110-layer network but has worse CIFAR-10 test error. The authors attribute this to overfitting and to the network being unnecessarily large for the small dataset.
The authors do not use strong regularization such as maxout or dropout, and say that combining it with their method may improve CIFAR-10 results, which they leave for future work.
For the MS COCO experiments, multi-scale training was not performed because of limited time; multi-scale testing was used instead.
